Welcome to the Intelligence Brief for Sunday, May 10, 2026. I'm Andrew.
And I'm Aria. We have a fascinating day of signals today — and there is a single thread connecting most of them.

Let's start with the most-debated story of the day. Bun's experimental Rust rewrite hit 99.8% test compatibility on Linux x64 glibc. 496 HN points, but 463 comments — that's a 0.93 comment-to-point ratio. Nearly every person who upvoted also argued.
Wait — the branch is literally named claude/phase-a-port. Claude rewrote 760,000 lines of Zig into Rust across 43 commits and it passes 99.8% of the test suite?
That's the number. And the community is processing whether 0.2% failure is negligible or critical. But structurally: a team of engineers would spend months on this. An AI agent did phase one in days.
OK but here's what I keep thinking about — Zig has a formal ban on LLM contributions. So Bun can't upstream this. They did a 760K-line port that can never go back to the project it came from.
Which makes it more of a stress test than a production migration. And the community is debating exactly that: does 99.8% passing count as 'done,' or does the 0.2% live in the worst paths?
I think the honest answer is: no one knows yet. And that uncertainty is exactly why the ratio was so high. This is genuinely new territory.

Let's move to the day's highest-scoring story: a Fields Medal winner's experience with ChatGPT 5.5 Pro. Timothy Gowers — one of the world's top combinatorialists — evaluated the model on frontier math problems.
A Fields Medal winner testing an AI on the hardest open problems in his field. That's the most credible possible evaluator. What did he find?

The community is split on interpretation. The consensus is that the model impressed him. But the 0.72:1 ratio says 451 people were actively debating whether it's genuine reasoning or pattern-matching at high resolution.
That's the core question, right? If you train on every solved math paper ever written, can you cross-domain pattern-match to produce something that looks like novel reasoning?
Gowers is qualified to distinguish between those — and he's not dismissing the model. That's the signal. When a Fields Medal winner says 'this impressed me,' practitioners take that seriously.
OK so let me connect this to the Bun story. Both are asking the same question from different angles: what does it mean that AI-generated output passes the most rigorous tests we have for correctness?
Exactly. A test suite at 99.8%, and a mathematician's evaluation of novel reasoning. Two different quality bars, both cleared. The community is processing both simultaneously.
Internet Archive expanding to Switzerland. 585 HN points, 88 comments — the 0.15:1 ratio is near-pure endorsement. The community read it, upvoted it, and shared it without needing to argue.
That makes sense. The Archive is the internet's memory. Getting it into Swiss jurisdiction means a single legal system can't take it down. That's infrastructure redundancy for human knowledge.

A key ArXiv paper today: LLMs corrupt your documents when you delegate. 385 points. The finding is that the corruption is systematic, not random — it concentrates around numerical data and qualified statements.
Oh that's actually worse than random. If errors were random, you'd catch them with variance. Systematic corruption means your pipeline is consistently wrong in the same direction.
The production implication is that you can't just review the output. You have to validate output against the source document explicitly, for every category of content that LLMs statistically corrupt.
Add that to your AI infrastructure checklist. Don't just review — validate against source.

On the GitHub trending side, we saw three repos describing a new agent stack layer: addyosmani's agent-skills at 22.8K stars, nexu-io's open-design at 28K, and ByteDance's UI-TARS-desktop gaining 801 stars today.

Engineering skills, design systems, and GUI automation. That's actually a complete layer cake. Agent tells you what to build, design system tells you what it should look like, UI-TARS executes it on screen.
The community is voting for each layer as it arrives. That's codification — the phase where informal tools become infrastructure.
And the Lobsters signal: 'Just Fucking Use Go' at 173 points — the platform's top story. No benchmarks, no comparisons. Just pick Go and ship.
The same community fascinated by the Bun Zig-to-Rust AI port is also voting overwhelmingly for the essay that says: stop optimizing your language choice and build something.
Those aren't in tension. They're the same insight at different levels. The AI is doing the migration work so you don't have to. And the practitioner's job is to ship, not to deliberate.

Today's thesis: AI agents are passing the hardest correctness tests we know how to apply — a runtime test suite, a mathematician's evaluation, a 760K-line migration. The community's job now is to figure out what that means for the work we do.
The practitioner move: start validating your AI-assisted document pipelines against source. Study what Gowers actually said. And pick your language — then build.
That's the brief for May 10th. See you tomorrow.
